steps: Connect Gain before the stage that needs more headroom, then add a Meter downstream.
Start at 0 dB. Play a representative loud passage and reduce Gain by 3–6 dB if the next stage is overloaded.
Compare at the same monitoring volume. Increase only while the downstream peak has room.
gain.success: The level changes while rhythm and tone stay the same. A −6 dB cut roughly halves sample amplitude.
gain.check: If distortion remains after a cut, inspect the source and earlier stages: attenuation cannot restore samples already clipped.
gain.listen: Compare Input reference with Output. The drum-and-bass phrase keeps its timing as Gain changes.

steps: Place Volume on the branch you want to balance before it joins other sources.
Begin at 100%, then lower that branch while the other source plays.
Use 0% for silence and restore the prior percentage when finished.
volume.success: 50% is half amplitude, about −6 dB; 200% doubles amplitude and needs headroom.
volume.check: If turning this down changes the wrong sound, follow its incoming wire to confirm which branch it controls.
volume.listen: Use the same phrase to compare 50%, 100% and 200%. Output changes level without changing pitch.

steps: Begin with Bass and Treble at 0 dB so the shelves are flat.
For boom, try Bass −3 dB and move Bass frequency lower to focus on the bottom rather than all low mids.
For brightness, try Treble +2 dB. Raise Treble frequency to affect mainly the upper end.
Match output loudness before comparing Bypass; check headroom after boosts.
bassTreble.success: Shelves change broad regions. Frequency moves the transition; it is not a separate gain adjustment.
bassTreble.check: If voice sounds thin or harsh, reduce the amount or move the transition away from important voice frequencies.
bassTreble.listen: The fixture combines bass, bell harmonics and broadband texture. Listen for low weight versus high brightness, rather than overall loudness alone.

steps: Start with all ten bands at 0 dB and identify a specific problem by listening.
Read the band descriptions below; change one relevant fader by 1–3 dB.
Compare Input reference with Output, then check neighboring bands only if the correction needs a broader shape.
After boosts, check downstream peaks and reduce upstream Gain if necessary.
graphicEq.success: Each fixed band shapes an overlapping region: low faders affect weight, middle faders body and articulation, high faders brightness.
graphicEq.check: A 16 kHz boost may be barely audible on your hardware. Do not compensate by adding extreme gain; use material containing that range.
graphicEq.listen: Bass notes, low rumble, bell overtones and quiet broadband texture give the ten bands material to work on. Each band's purpose and tradeoff is explained below.

steps: Add a band and choose its job: Peaking for a local correction, a shelf for a broad region, or High/Low pass to remove a frequency extreme.
Select that band's point or row. Set Frequency, then Q for width/resonance; use Gain only on Peaking and shelves.
Toggle that band's Enabled control to compare its contribution before adding another.
Inspect the combined curve and downstream headroom. Keep the fewest bands that solve the problem.
parametricEq.success: The selected band's shape, location and width are distinguishable from the summed response. A flat All pass magnitude can still change phase.
parametricEq.check: If Gain does nothing, check the filter type: pass, notch and All pass filters do not use that gain control.
parametricEq.listen: Edit any of four example bands, then switch listening between Input and Output. Browser biquads demonstrate the selected shapes; the curve is illustrative rather than an engine measurement.

steps: Play both quiet and loud phrases. Begin with Threshold −18 dBFS, Ratio 3:1, Attack 10 ms and Release 150 ms.
Lower Threshold until loud phrases show useful reduction; keep quiet phrases natural.
Adjust Attack to preserve or tame beginnings and Release so recovery does not pump between syllables.
Add Makeup only enough to match the bypassed listening level.
compressor.success: Loud passages move closer to quiet ones. Ratio changes the level above threshold, while Makeup lifts the whole result.
compressor.check: If it only sounds louder, return Makeup to 0 dB and compare again. If reduction is constant, raise Threshold or lower the input.
compressor.listen: A pulsing tone arrives in four level sections. Compare the loud third section with the quieter first, then change Threshold and Ratio; this is a simplified envelope compressor.

steps: Measure the background while quiet, then the quietest speech you want to keep.
Set Threshold between those levels and start with a modest Range such as 20 dB.
Increase Hold or Release if word endings disappear; lower Threshold if quiet words never open the gate.
Use Hysteresis to stop rapid reopening near the boundary; use Ratio for gentler downward expansion.
gate.success: Background drops during pauses while wanted phrases open the gate. A gate cannot remove noise underneath speech.
gate.check: If it chatters, increase Hysteresis/Hold before deepening Range. If the first consonant is cut, shorten Attack or lower Threshold.
gate.listen: Voice-like synthetic phrases sit above a quiet bed. Listen to the pauses and word tails; compare Input with the attenuated Output.

steps: Put Limiter after boosts and mixing, near the end of the audible path.
Start with Ceiling −1 dBFS, Lookahead 5 ms and Release 100 ms.
Play the loudest expected passage and check peak limiting.
Reduce upstream levels if limiting is continuous; use Compressor for routine dynamic control.
limiter.success: Occasional sample peaks are contained while most material passes. A sample-peak ceiling is not a true-peak loudness guarantee.
limiter.check: If everything sounds flattened, reduce the level feeding the limiter instead of continually lowering Ceiling.
limiter.listen: The third section contains deliberately oversized peaks. The bounded example shows a sample ceiling and release, not the production lookahead algorithm.

steps: Use a repeatable event such as a recorded clap to decide which path arrives early.
Insert Sync on that earlier path and begin at 0 ms.
Add the measured positive offset in small steps, then compare the recorded result again.
delay.success: The entire signal arrives later with the same shape. This tool does not mix in a dry copy or create an echo effect.
delay.check: If audio already arrives late, adding delay makes that worse. Adjust the earlier path or the other system's timing.
delay.listen: Try 300 ms and compare Input reference with Output at the same timeline position. The first output is silent until the delayed source arrives.

steps: Begin at 0 Semitones and 0 Cents.
Try a small shift such as −2 semitones, then listen through a whole phrase.
Use Cents for fine adjustment. Check clarity and latency before using a large interval.
pitch.success: Musical pitch changes while the phrase duration remains the same; +12 semitones is one octave.
pitch.check: If intelligibility suffers, reduce the shift and compare the unprocessed source. Large shifts can expose artifacts.
pitch.listen: A synthesized bell melody is regenerated at the new pitch with exactly the original note timing. This teaches interval and timing, not the engine's pitch-shifting artifacts.

steps: Identify whether the unwanted fundamental is near 50 or 60 Hz.
Set that Frequency, start with Amount 50% and a small harmonic count.
Add harmonics only where higher buzz remains, then compare lower voice notes or bass for damage.
dehum.success: Narrow notches reduce the fundamental and selected multiples while leaving most surrounding sound alone.
dehum.check: If the buzz remains, verify its frequency. Broadband hiss needs a different treatment; more notches can remove wanted low notes.
dehum.listen: The input contains a known 60 Hz hum with eight harmonics. Compare 50 versus 60 Hz and change the harmonic count to hear why matching matters.

steps: Loop a passage containing an isolated unwanted click and wanted sharp sounds.
Start at Threshold 50%, then lower it gradually if the click remains.
Raise Threshold if consonants or percussion become dull.
declick.success: Exceptional short impulses are reduced while ordinary attacks remain recognizable.
declick.check: Persistent gaps, clipping or driver dropouts require fixing the source; a click repair tool cannot reconstruct missing passages.
declick.listen: Several short injected impulses interrupt synthetic phrases. The lesson repairs only those known impulses when they cross the threshold; it does not reproduce the engine's detector.

steps: Play the route and keep the wanted source quiet.
Click Learn noise while only the steady room/fan background is present, then Stop learning and keep profile.
Resume speech and adjust Reduction. Raise Noise left if speech becomes watery.
Relearn after moving the mic or changing the background.
denoise.success: The learned background drops, including under phrases, without excessive damage to wanted detail.
denoise.check: If the profile contains speech, learn it again in silence. Increasing Reduction cannot repair a contaminated profile.
denoise.listen: The lesson starts with a prepared synthetic hiss profile. It attenuates a separately known noise layer, not a real spectral-subtraction implementation; use it to compare reduction and residual noise.

steps: Place Speech Denoise before stages that amplify noise.
Start at Strength 70% and speak normally, including quiet syllables.
Reduce Strength if breathing, consonants or desired ambience become unnatural.
speechDenoise.success: Background is reduced around conversational speech without a manual Learn step.
speechDenoise.check: For music or delicate material, compare Bypass carefully; a speech-oriented cleaner may suppress sound you want to keep.
speechDenoise.listen: Synthetic voice-like phrases and hiss demonstrate stronger versus gentler cleanup. The known noise layer is attenuated for teaching; this is not the production speech detector.

steps: Learn a noise-only interval, then keep the profile before evaluating speech.
Start with Threshold 3 dB above the learned noise and Reduction 40 dB.
Lower Threshold or Reduction if quiet syllables develop holes; relearn when the noise changes.
spectralGate.success: Frequency regions close to the learned background are attenuated; this differs from closing the entire signal with Gate.
spectralGate.check: A profile learned during speech can remove wanted frequencies. Correct the profile before applying stronger settings.
spectralGate.listen: A prepared noise layer makes threshold and blocked-region reduction audible. This deliberately simplified separation model does not simulate FFT bins or production artifacts.

steps: Choose and approve an impulse-response WAV in the actual FIR inspector.
Wait for the prepared response and inspect its duration, partitions and fixed latency.
Begin with Wet 100% and Gain 0 dB. Compare against dry at matched loudness, then blend if useful.
If loading fails, inspect the file/error before saving the intended route.
firFilter.success: The source is convolved with the loaded response. Wet/Dry blends aligned paths; output Gain adjusts the result.
firFilter.check: A long or strongly colored response can smear attacks or increase level. Check the IR and headroom before blaming the source.
firFilter.listen: Browser convolution uses a short built-in multi-tap response, not your file. Compare Dry with Wet to hear the tail; the actual inspector's load/prepare/partition workflow is described below.

steps: Put Mute on the specific branch you want to silence.
Select Muted and verify its downstream meter falls silent.
Restore the signal deliberately when ready; other branches retain their own states.
mute.success: Only audio through this node is silenced; it does not act as a global microphone toggle.
mute.check: If another source remains audible, trace its separate path. Do not assume one mute controls every input.
mute.listen: Input reference remains available for comparison even when Output is muted. This audition choice affects only the lesson monitor.

steps: Connect the two alternative sources to the switch.
Choose the source to hear and select a fade suitable for the transition.
Switch while both sources are active and listen through the whole fade.
inputSwitch.success: One source replaces the other through a transition; this is not a permanent sum like Mixer.
inputSwitch.check: If the chosen input is silent, check its incoming source before repeatedly switching.
inputSwitch.listen: Input A is drums/bass; Input B is a bell melody. Listen to either reference separately, then Output while changing selection. Slow fade lasts two seconds in this example.

steps: Wire music through Duck as the target.
Choose a separate voice node as the trigger; the key controls attenuation and is not mixed into Duck's output.
Set Threshold so speech triggers the detector, then adjust Amount for the music reduction.
Tune Attack, Hold and Release to bridge short pauses. Mix voice downstream only if you want it in the final output.
duck.success: Music lowers during key phrases and recovers afterward. Changing music level alone should not be your speech trigger.
duck.check: If music never ducks, verify the trigger node and its level against Threshold. If voice is missing from the final mix, connect its audible branch separately.
duck.listen: Input A is music; the trigger reference is a different voice-like phrase with pauses. Output contains only music following that key. Audition the key separately to understand the timing.

steps: Set a buffer long enough for the history you need and start the route.
Let history accumulate, then Pause or seek within the available range.
Resume from history and use the live-edge action when you want current audio again.
timeShift.success: The source keeps advancing while playback reads retained history. History before the retained window is unavailable.
timeShift.check: If you cannot seek far enough back, check buffer capacity and how long the route has run.
timeShift.listen: The fixed story is live for two seconds, paused for one, then behind live, then back live at six seconds. The output waveform shows the gap and replayed content.

steps: Connect each wanted source to the same Mixer; its input rows follow the upstream connections.
Play sources separately to identify their rows, then set their individual volumes.
Play both together and check the summed output. Lower the inputs if their combined peaks overload the next stage.
mixer.success: Both different tracks are audible in Output and each volume changes only its own contribution. 100% + 100% can exceed available headroom.
mixer.check: If one fader appears ineffective, listen to that input reference alone and verify its wire/source is active.
mixer.listen: A syncopated drum-and-bass track and a higher bell melody have different rhythms and spectra. Set either fader to zero to isolate the other; both raw input waveforms stay visible.

steps: Place Meter before or after the stage you want to inspect.
Read the stereo RMS bars for average energy, white current-peak markers for transients and gold held peaks for recent extremes.
Check the clipping count and downstream headroom while playing the loudest passage.
meter.success: Meter passes audio unchanged. RMS is generally below peak; held peaks let you catch events you missed visually.
meter.check: Silence at this meter points upstream. Healthy signal here but silence later points to a downstream route, mute or device.
meter.listen: Four level sections include an intentionally over-range third section. The lesson's bar, current peak, held peak and clip count are computed from the same stereo samples you hear, before the quiet browser monitor gain.

steps: Choose the exact microphone or capture endpoint in Properties; do not leave the device unchosen.
Select Mono, Stereo, Left or Right to match how that device is wired.
Save the route, Play and check the input meter while making a sound.
physicalInput.success: Only the explicitly chosen capture device supplies this branch. Left/Right can select a microphone present on just one side.
physicalInput.check: Check Windows permission, device availability and channel choice. A missing mic must be rebound deliberately.
physicalInput.listen: This diagram explains channel selection only. It never opens your microphone or invents a browser recording of the selected device.

steps: Choose the intended render endpoint explicitly in Properties.
Wire the processed branch to it, Save and Play at a low monitoring level.
Check the route meter and the chosen Windows output's volume/mute state.
physicalOutput.success: The branch reaches that output device. Choosing an output does not select a capture device.
physicalOutput.check: If meters move but nothing is audible, confirm the endpoint, Windows volume and physical connection. Avoid a loop back into the same captured output.
physicalOutput.listen: The diagram shows destination selection without accessing your speakers or claiming to verify a real route.

steps: Open the application and make it play audio.
Refresh the running-app list and choose the intended process in Tools.
Add the source, connect it to your processing/output, Save and Play.
Check the source meter while the selected app makes sound.
applicationCapture.success: The selected application's audio enters the route independently of a whole-output loopback.
applicationCapture.check: A restarted app can have a new process identity. Refresh and select it deliberately; check whether the target app is actually producing sound.
applicationCapture.listen: This process-selection diagram is visual only; the website cannot inspect or capture your running applications.

steps: Choose the Windows render endpoint whose playback you want to capture.
Play audio to that endpoint, then wire Loopback to your intended route.
Choose a separate monitoring destination or a layout that avoids feeding captured audio back into itself.
endpointLoopback.success: The endpoint's combined playback is captured, rather than a single application's process.
endpointLoopback.check: If the signal repeats or grows, stop the route and remove the feedback path. If silent, verify where Windows is sending playback.
endpointLoopback.listen: The diagram distinguishes whole-endpoint capture from app capture; it performs no browser loopback capture.

steps: Install/enable the intended cable using Virtual Cables and identify its render/capture names.
In the sending app, choose the cable's render endpoint as playback.
Choose that cable source in AudioRouter, connect processing/output, Save and Play.
virtualRenderSource.success: Audio sent by the app to the cable becomes an AudioRouter input. Direction is from app playback into the route.
virtualRenderSource.check: Confirm the cable identity and sending app's playback selection; similarly named physical endpoints are not the same cable.
virtualRenderSource.listen: The direction diagram explains the Windows/app boundary without installing or opening a virtual device.

steps: Choose the intended installed cable sink in AudioRouter and wire your processed branch to it.
In the receiving app, choose that cable's capture endpoint as its microphone/input.
Save and Play the route, then check the receiving app's input meter.
virtualCaptureSink.success: Processed AudioRouter audio appears as input to the other app. It does not automatically play through speakers.
virtualCaptureSink.check: If the app hears the raw microphone, change that app's selected input to the cable capture endpoint.
virtualCaptureSink.listen: The diagram teaches route-to-app direction. It does not access your apps or alter Windows defaults.

steps: Add Test Signal and start at a quiet Level such as −24 dBFS.
Choose Frequency and Duration for a repeatable check.
Connect only the path you intend to test, Save and Play. Check meters before raising monitoring volume.
testSignal.success: A known source helps separate processing/routing faults from capture-device problems. It has no microphone input.
testSignal.check: If the meter sees the tone but the destination does not, inspect the downstream path. Avoid loud continuous tones.
testSignal.listen: Frequency and Level control an actual generated sine. The website lesson uses an eight-second source for the shared timeline; the app's Duration sets the real test length.

steps: Choose and approve the local file in the actual Audio File inspector.
Connect the player to the intended processing and output, then Save the route.
Use its Play/Pause/Stop/Seek controls; compare a repeatable passage when tuning effects.
audioFile.success: Pause keeps the position, Stop returns to the start, and seeking chooses a deliberate point in the file.
audioFile.check: If loading fails, inspect format/path access. A browser lesson playing successfully does not prove your local file is supported.
audioFile.listen: A built-in synthetic melody stands in for a file so you can practice play, pause and seek. No user's file is read or uploaded.

steps: Wire the branch to record into Recorder and choose/approve a recording folder before the first take.
Save and Play the session, then press Record. Recording is a separate deliberate action unless Auto record is enabled.
Press Stop to finalize the take, find it in Recording, and play the completed file.
Check the saved file and branch before relying on a long take; set splitting only when useful.
recorder.success: Capture activity stays at Recorder; completed-file playback belongs to Audio File. Stopping finalizes the interval actually recorded.
recorder.check: If no take starts, check the approved folder, session state and connected branch. A running route alone does not mean recording is active.
recorder.listen: Press Record example, stop after a few seconds, then Play recording. Only that in-memory synthetic interval is replayed; there is no microphone, disk write or download.

steps: On PC A, connect a source to Network Send and enter PC B's literal IP address.
On PC B, add Network Receive with PC A's sender address and connect it to an output.
Match the UDP port and privately copied generated pairing key on both PCs.
Save and Play both routes, then inspect receiver activity and output.
networkSend.success: Pairing precedes packet flow. The receiver is another AudioRouter on another PC; the sender running does not prove successful reception.
networkSend.check: Check address direction, matching port/key, firewall access and receiver state before increasing buffers.
networkSend.listen: The first 2.4 seconds show pairing with no received audio. Then a delayed copy crosses the illustrated network to PC B. This is a local timing model with no packets or remote connection.

steps: On PC B, enter the literal address of the sending PC in Sender and choose the receiving UDP port.
Match the sender's port and pairing key; connect Receive to a local output.
Save and Play both PCs. Begin with Buffer 40 ms and inspect incoming activity.
Increase Buffer only if timing variation causes gaps; recheck the added delay.
networkReceive.success: Only the configured sender/key feeds this source. More buffer trades latency for tolerance to packet timing variation.
networkReceive.check: No received packets usually means address, key, port or firewall; a larger buffer cannot fix mismatched pairing.
networkReceive.listen: Pairing completes before received sound starts at PC B. Increase Buffer and compare with the sender reference to hear the extra local simulated delay; no real network is used.

steps: Scan an explicitly chosen installed x64 plugin directory and inspect a supported result.
Add the intended exact plugin to the draft and wire it into the branch.
Save and Play, then verify plugin running telemetry and the downstream meter.
Use the plugin-defined parameter ranges and matched-level Bypass comparisons.
plugin.success: The chosen plugin identity and its own parameter metadata determine the controls. A scan result alone does not prove successful live processing.
plugin.check: If it faults, inspect the error and recover deliberately. Protected voice paths remain silent rather than silently bypassing a failed processor.
plugin.listen: A generic website sound cannot demonstrate an arbitrary installed plugin. This page uses a visual lifecycle explanation and teaches how to verify the real effect.

steps: Add a Group from Tools and move/resize it behind related nodes.
Click its name to rename it, choose a readable color and keep background opacity subtle.
Lock the finished region to prevent accidental movement while working nearby.
group.success: A named region makes the route easier to read. Audio still follows the existing wires; the rectangle is not an audio processor.
group.check: If moving or resizing is unavailable, check Locked. Keep the caption away from controls and wires.
group.listen: This organizational diagram has no relevant audio example. Grouping changes canvas presentation only.

steps: Add Fun Voice Changer after your microphone tools and before the output Discord uses as its microphone.
Choose a preset, press Play and talk; the inspector shows the note it hears while pitch stages run.
Adjust the preset's sliders, or open the sections below for every setting. Reset to preset restores the recipe.
funVoiceChanger.success: Your voice comes out as the chosen character, at about the same loudness as your normal voice, 21 ms later.
funVoiceChanger.check: If the effect sounds broken in Discord, turn Discord's noise suppression off for the cable input. If pitch correction warbles, lower the noise gate or add Denoise before the tool.
funVoiceChanger.listen: A synthetic sung voice is regenerated with the chosen pitch and formant, then given the ring buzz. It teaches what each control changes, not the engine's exact sound.
